content:
I realized that Charlie Munger created the business equivalent of "the game" (the one you just lost, because you thought about it) 



It's whether you approach a problem by starting with the incentives. 

In Charlie's words, “Never, ever, think about something else when you should be thinking about the power of incentives.”

I had 3 mini-realizations about this today after I remembered the Charlie quote: 

- Customer not reading your support docs? Incentives. 
- Leads not moving quickly through the pipeline? Incentives (yours and theirs). 
- Hard problems getting set aside for more visible quick wins? Incentives.

It seems like the first question to ask any sort of systems-level problem is "what are the incentives at play?"

A thread that you keep pulling and pulling. 

Also Charlie: "Well, I think I’ve been in the top 5% of my age cohort all my life in understanding the power of incentives, and all my life I’ve underestimated it."

"The business game" is just remembering that incentives drive the world. 

The business version of the phrase

"don't attribute to malice what can be attributed to ignorance" 

is just 

“don't attribute to nearly anything else what can be attributed to incentives".

content:
Cross-team level-up: when you make a decision that impacts another person or team (aka 95% of them), write down the factors that lead to the decision in a decision log. Bullet points are great. 

Most of the cross-functional disagreements will be preemptively solved when you share your thinking. Disagreements often stem from a lack of shared context, not fundamentally different beliefs. 

Doing this also opens up the best case scenario: your teammates disagree, they accurately refute an assumption or belief, propose an unconsidered alternative, and help improve the strategy or decision.

Last month, I re-subscribed to some daily news emails. I'm now more informed about world events. But the daily digest of everything going wrong in the world can really sour the calm headspace of the morning. 

There are practical benefits to “being informed”. There are also hidden costs.

Seems like a tradeoff of looking stupid when someones asks for your opinion on XYZ event vs avoiding the constant stream of drama. If that's the trade, I’ll take the moments of perceived stupidity anytime. It reminds me Taleb: 

“Much of what other people know isn’t worth knowing.”

Today, I started to wonder why I was even reading the news when there are hundreds of high-quality books that I've never opened the cover of. 

I'm unsure if a daily news habit is getting me closer to that Naval idea of a "fit body, a calm mind, a house full of love". 

Maybe I should take a page out of Warren & Charlie's playbook and read more books instead. It's as Charlie put it himself: 

"In my whole life, I have known no wise people (over a broad subject matter area) who didn't read all the time - none, zero."

I have to assume Charlie wasn't talking about daily email newsletters.

content:
Tobi's AI memo has me thinking of the ways to max adoption across an operations stack:  


[1] New employee onboarding *must* include shipping an AI-augmented prototype. Deliver it as a quick win in the first week. Forces familiarity with your stack and how to map LLMs back to your problem space. 

[2] Monthly vendor review, with transactions pulled directly from your ledger, choosing from {leave it, churn it, negotiate it}. Export some messy dataset from Quickbooks or similar, have an agent reason on whether that level of spend makes sense given your headcount and value it creates. 

[3] Introduce new gates to pass before hiring a new role: try it with routine automation -> deploy custom agent -> find alternative path to create capacity for a current 10x employee to own it -> hire net-new talent. 

[4] Ensure that prompt libraries are shared across your company. Great prompts = intellectual property, make them accessible. (Note: I don't see OpenAI doing a great job at this, I'm looking elsewhere for Integral and just signed us up with Perplexity). 

[5] Snapshot your ARR:FTE ratios over time. Simple google doc with some HRIS data. Drive it up and to the right. Repeat the loop of {automate -> leverage -> ARR -> growth capital -> automate ... }. This isn't an impetus to reduce headcount. It's a metric that demonstrates your capacity to create company-wide leverage. 

[6] Invest in tools that index company knowledge. Build a graph (with proper access controls) that saves hours manually crawling google docs and slack. Getting huge value from Convictional for internal knowledge and Plain on the support side.

[7] Prioritize and celebrate learning velocity. So many ways to be improving now, with the possibility for AI-enabled demo reviews, design crits, negotiation playbacks, and even VC-level feedback on board memo drafts. Worth asking the question "does teammate X have an AI-enabled coach?".

content:
"How To Be Successful" by  Sam Altman is like a testimony of Sam's personal playbook over the last decade (worked out well imo). The big ideas: 

1. 📈 Compound yourself -> "Exponential curves are the key to wealth generation." 

2. 💪 Have almost too much self-belief -> "The most successful people I know believe in themselves almost to the point of delusion" 

3. 🤔 Learn to think independently -> "'I will fail many times, and I will be really right once' is the entrepreneurs’ way."

4. 🗣️ Get good at “sales” -> "The best way to be good at sales is to genuinely believe in what you’re selling" 

5. 🎲 Make it easy to take risks -> "Most people overestimate risk and underestimate reward." 

6. 🎯 Focus -> "Almost everyone I’ve ever met would be well-served by spending more time thinking about what to focus on."

7. 💼 Work hard -> "As in most cases, momentum compounds, and success begets success." 

8. 🚀 Be bold ->"If you are making progress on an important problem, you will have a constant tailwind of people wanting to help you." 

9. 🔥 Be willful -> "A big secret is that you can bend the world to your will a surprising percentage of the time." 

10. 🛡️ Be hard to compete with -> "The best way to become difficult to compete with is to build up leverage." (ah, the L word, my favorite)

11. 🤝 Build a network -> "An effective way to build a network is to help people as much as you can" + "Be overly generous with sharing the upside; it will come back to you 10x"

12. 🏠 You get rich by owning things -> "The best way to make things that increase rapidly in value is by making things people want at scale."

13. 🔄 Be internally driven -> "Eventually, you will define your success by performing excellent work in areas that are important to you. The sooner you can start off in that direction, the further you will be able to go."

content:
The sticky note above my desk used to say "Q1 Goals." ... until I trashed it and felt relieved. 

For the last several years, I've done the January resolutions ritual: 
- Write down goals. 
- Visualize the outcome. 
- Pin sticky notes in every room of the house. 

The part I missed was that if you're already an overthinker, then constantly having goals shoved in your face can paralyze you. 

I can think a problem to death ("paralysis by analysis"). I might not find the solution, but I can guarantee myself a headache! 

This year, I wondered if there was a better way. A way to just *be* without relying sticky notes to tell me where to focus my energy.

By sheer luck, I found the Founders episode interviewing Patrick O'Shaughnessy. Patrick published an essay called "Growth without Goals" that completely rewired my thinking and encouraged me to trash the sticky notes. 

Two ideas that resonated: 

[1] "I wanted to write a book. Rather, I wanted to have written a book because I could carve a notch on my achievement belt ... Now I just want to explore." 

It feels exciting to write lofty goals and picture yourself achieving them. I can get JACKED UP thinking about what is possible. 

But the next day, the excitement wanes, and I'm left wondering whether I actually want the inputs that are needed to create the output - or if I just want the output itself. 

[2] "The key isn't thinking long-term, which implies long-term goals. Long-term thinking is really just goalless thinking. Long-term success probably just comes from an emphasis on process and mindset in the present."

I'm realizing that being so focused on future outcomes can make me forget to pay attention to what I'm doing right now. 

So I'm trying something new. No set goals this year. Just showing up, exploring, focusing on the process, leaning into whatever draws me in.

If sticky notes aren't doing it for you, the essay is worth a read.

content:
Robert Greene compressed centuries of wisdom into a single life. Biggest ideas: 

[1] Find Your Life's Task

"At your birth a seed is planted. That seed is your uniqueness. It wants to grow, transform itself, and flower to its full potential. It has a natural, assertive energy to it. Your Life’s Task is to bring that seed to flower, to express your uniqueness through your work. You have a destiny to fulfill." 

Everyone has a purpose they are drawn towards. Identifying it is the hard part. Our life's work gets drowned out by social media, friends, parents, and a society that frowns upon uniqueness. 

Pursuing your life's work is the ultimate task, everything else is noise. 

[2] Craft A Grand Strategy 

"Grand strategy is the art of looking beyond the present battle and calculating ahead. Focus on your ultimate goal and plot to reach it.” 

Setting ambitious goals creates the direction that carries us. Look beyond immediate challenges and focus on your ultimate objective. The world won't accommodate you; you must shape it to your vision. 

[3] Cultivate An Aura Of Mystery

"There is too little mystery in the world; too many people say exactly what they feel or want."

By not revealing every thought and emotion, you create anticipation and curiosity. Others are engaged and intrigued by your next move. A hint of vagueness can mask the grander plan and draws others into your worldview. 

[4] Avoid Appearing Perfect 

"Appearing better than others is always dangerous, but most dangerous of all is to appear to have no faults or weaknesses. Envy creates silent enemies. It is smart to occasionally display defects, and admit to harmless vices, in order to deflect envy ... Only gods and the dead can seem perfect with impunity.”  

Envy drags on your potential. Better to avoid it altogether by showing small defects that make you relatable. Perfect is despised, humility is loved. 

[5] Ignore The Envy 

As a counterpoint, envy is inevitable for the successful. Jealousy is ingrained into human nature. The pettiness of others must not impact the pursuit of bigger goals.  

“When you show yourself to the world and display your talents, you naturally stir all kinds of resentment, envy, and other manifestations of insecurity...you cannot spend your life worrying about the petty feelings of others.”

[6] Action Above All (Practice Matters) 

If you learn a craft and can come to master it, it can bring you a far greater pleasure than any kind of drug or socializing. The timescale is years and decades -- whatever the craft, you need to invest the 10,000 hours for it to become second nature. 

You have to be patient, not be afraid of boredom, not be afraid of the effort. 

[7] Be Formless

The 48th law of 48 Laws of Power is to adapt to the circumstances around you. 

"Accept the fact that nothing is certain and no law is fixed. The best way to protect yourself is to be fluid and formless as water; never bet on stability or lasting order. Everything changes."

The best prioritization framework I've seen is LNO from Shreyas Doshi. 

Why? Because it force-ranks your day towards leverage. 

Each of us have mountains of things to do (handed out by others), half of which are overdue tasks or underdeveloped ideas. Our TODO lists grow so long that we need a TODO to simply read the whole TODO list.

But most TODOs are minutiae. This is not where the leverage is found. 

Leverage is in the 1 or 2 initiatives we can tackle today that can create an outsized impact. It's like if you applied that Sam Altman quote at a daily level: 

"But I always want it to be a project that, if successful, will make the rest of my career look like a footnote"

LNO is better than any email system, AI chief of staff, or wall of sticky notes, because it forces us to admit that most of the action items don't matter. 

A 10X career is born from executing 10x projects, again and again and again.

content:
A fun challenge of early stage startups: recognizing you're in desperate need of a skillset, and then taking it upon yourself to level up in that area. 

Last week, I did a speed run on PeopleOps. The goal was to land on a checklist that the Integral leads team could use to identify shortcomings in our process. 

My thesis is that high-quality repeated process will drive our target outcomes. 

After all, “You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.” ~ James Clear

The fastest path would be learning from the greats. People who have advised or scaled teams in the recent past and are masters in their crafts. And with only a week, I needed to think in chapters, not entire books. 

The trifecta I landed on:

1. The Great CEO Within ~ Matt Mochary 
2. High Growth Handbook ~ Elad Gil
3. Scaling People ~ Claire Hughes Johnson

These break down into 3 areas: Leadership Process, Recruiting, Management

### Leadership Processes ### 
(Adapted from Matt's "The Great CEO Within)

- Each function has clear OKRs or goals for the time period being measured against.
- Non-urgent, important topics are solicited at least 24 hours before the meeting.
- For leads meetings, all major comments are made in the doc 6+ hours before the meeting.
- Each action item has a clear owner assigned to it. Any unactioned items must have an explanation for them the following week, including any requests for assistance.
- Meeting notes are scrubbed of sensitive information and then pushed out to the broader team within 24hrs of the meeting occurring.
- Consistent structure for internal reporting on progress (ARR, burn ratio)


### Recruiting ### 
(Content largely from Elad's "High Growth Handbook") 

- Hire a recruiter (who owns sourcing and the process, not giving offers)
- Ask every candidate the same questions during interviewing.
- Assign interviews specific focus areas during the interview.
- Check each candidate’s references
- Have a consistent candidate onboarding process -> a week-long onboarding journey, personalized welcome letter, buddy system, 30/60/90 goals, and a clear path to getting a "quick win" in their first week 

### Management ### 
(From Claire's "Scaling People") 

You and individual reports
- Hold 1:1s on a weekly or biweekly cadence, and they are never cancelled, only rescheduled.
- Create agendas for your 1:1s that include contributions from both sides, notes, and agreed-upon actions.
- Have quarterly goals that you track together.
- Hold bidirectional feedback sessions with your reports every 3 to 6 months.
- Hold formal performance conversations every 3, 6, or 12 months (the more rapidly your company is changing, the more often these should occur) that emphasize both the results the person achieved (or didn’t) and how the person did or did not achieve those results.

content:
"Most companies have more ideas than they have ability or resources to implement" ~Colin Bryar (formerly Jeff Bezos's "Shadow" / chief of staff) 

This is especially true for early stage startups trying to move faster than they even think is possible. There's so much green field to experiment and explore. 

Too many bets to take, not enough hours in the day to play the hands. 

Bryar recommends building a process to "take the ideas, pick the best ones, refine them, and make sure you're only working on the best ideas that you think are possible". 

This is one of those ideas that, once it sinks in, changes how you operate. 

After all - a roadmap is just a series of bets to take. 

A backlog is just a list of things we could try to delight our customers (and may never take at all, that Q4 roadmap commitment be damned).

It's easy to get lost in the idea of grooming the backlog, scoping features to death, and working through the fancy prioritization framework of the month.

Product management is building your team's own unique process to turn a huge backlog of ideas into a prioritized list of the best possible next steps. 

Building that process can be intensely complicated - but it's the most important part of knowing what to deliver in order to win your market and turn your customers into champions.

content:
A 1940s advertising exec boiled down the creative process down to 5 steps - and used it to publish 70 patents in his lifetime. 

1. Observe: gather raw material. Learning and observing bring us the ideas that can be morphed into new combinations. Search for specific ideas ("how?") and general ideas ("why?"). 

2. Digest: fit the jigsaw puzzle together. Bring different ideas together in unique and novel ways. Novel takes on old ideas are where the gold lies ("what if I rented out my own apartment, or drove a stranger in my car?") 

3. Separate: create space for new perspectives. Drop the ideas from your mind altogether. There is magic in a long walk. Many great ideas are born in the shower, where there's no chance for technology to occupy our minds. 

4. Serendipity: let the new ideas come to you. Our subconscious mind is powerful yet unpredictable. The raw materials have been gathered, but we can't "think" our way to creativity. We must wait for the flash of insight.

5. Shaping: turn eureka into utility. Share the new insight with others who have no clue what you're talking about. Hear their feedback and incorporate it. Great ideas can sound crazy at the start - only by shaping them into something useful can others benefit from your creativity.

The most important skill to hone is good judgement

In archery, champions are measured in millimetres. Knowing where to aim is vital. 

The initial position of the arrow influences its trajectory over the meters that follow. 

Much is the same about growing a business, launching a new product, or honing a craft. 

Everyone can signup for chatGPT and crank out a blog post. Within product, there are custom GPTs for mockups, spitting out requirements docs, and tools to turn it all into a functioning codebase. 

But none of this matters without the judgment to identify the right customer, the right positioning, the right go-to-market, the right sequencing. 

Being able to identify the right target and the optimal path to take is one of the most valuable abilities to hone. 

As Naval said: “Leverage is a force multiplier for your judgment.”

As individual leverage increases by the week, judgement remains the difference between decent, good, and truly excellent.

content:
“What gets measured gets managed” — great idea that tends to fall down in an era of tools galore and rapid experimentation.

Dream case? All business data in a single data lake, cleaned, standardized, ready. 

Then you can really play ball: 

- profitability by project 
- gross margin by SKU
- revenue per atomic unit 

But the vision of a beautiful data lake is often just a dream. 

If we’re honest with ourselves - there’s usually a system or dataset that gets left out for a reason like “there’s no API to hit”

Imagine if a pizza shop measured profitability only using the cost of the crust, not the labor or toppings. 

The only thing the chef could do is say they need to move to thin crust - missing the entire rest of the production process. 

The truly data driven teams see the ROI in getting the relevant data into one place - especially since modern SaaS is a lot more complex than making pizza.

content:
Nobody knows how successful you are, so you may as well act as if you've already won. There's truth in "fake it til you make it". 

Yesterday I strategized with a fashion exec on the best brands to pitch for cross-brand partnerships. I asked her how she determined the legitimacy of other brands:

"It's more of an art than a science ... we look at website traffic, Instagram followers, product photography, y'know, a number of factors."

To which I replied, "That's fair, and I do the same, but it also sounds like there are times when you really have no idea."

"Yes ... yes, I guess you're right. It's tough to know. These all correlate, but there's no certainty. Success can be deceiving. Sometimes we just ask brands how well they're doing." 

This is someone who has built her founded her own brand, has tens of thousands of followers, and built a 7-figure business. 

If anyone should be able to judge how "successful" a brand is from the outside, it's her.

The truth is, nobody really knows how "successful" you are. They can look at some metrics, sure, but often they are waiting for you to tell them. Every question is a chance to write your own story. 

Why not tell it as if you're already winning?

Success in a VC-backed startup requires you to be a little crazy. 

[1] You’re in a company where barely anyone knows you ... yet on paper the company is worth millions.

[2] You cold email VPs at companies that your parents wished you worked at - and they actually reply!

[3] You’re a capital allocator with leverage across the raised funds, your time, and your team’s time. 

Anything you write in # general is read by the other capital allocators who can decide to change roadmap, pricing, or anything else within minutes. Try changing Walmart or JP Morgan’s roadmap. Try getting budget for anything more than a pencil at a BigCo. 

[4] The entire premise of your company is that you'll create a monopoly. 

Hit $100M ARR or fold. Even better, create an entirely new industry and be a monopoly by default. Playing small is the pathway to failure. 

Here's to the crazy ones.
